articles.title: That Sinking Feeling: A Race Against Time to Save a Pregnant Woman from a Car Submerged in Freezing Waters
articles.content:
Shedly Apollon was awakened by a sound she couldn’t possibly sleep through: that of her car splashing into a pond … with her in it. Add in the rush of cold water pooling beneath her feet, and suddenly Apollon was fully alert, if disoriented. She was also fearing for her life. Actually, two lives. Apollon was in her 34th week of pregnancy on that cold morning this past February in Stuart, Florida, when she awoke to the reality that she was trapped in a sinking car.
Apollon, of nearby Port St. Lucie, had been on her way to a prenatal massage gifted by her fiancé, Woodly Sully. It was a birthday present. (Yes, this happened on Apollon’s 29th birthday.) Apollon had been struggling during her third trimester with preeclampsia, and as she drove to the massage, she began to feel woozy. She pulled her silver 2019 Hyundai Elantra over to the shoulder of Interstate 95, called Sully to let him know what was happening, drank some water, ate a little food and waited for the dizziness to subside.
After it did, about 10 minutes later, she got back on the road, but what happened next is a blur. Her car’s safety systems were beeping, telling her she was veering outside her lane, although in her haze-filled mind she was driving perfectly straight. She tried to pull over again, but started passing out. “I thought the car was in park,” Apollon recalls, “but in reality, it was still in drive.” And she drove off the right side of the road, straight into the pond.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more true stories, history, cleaning, travel, tech, humor and fun facts all week long.
When she came to seconds later to the sound of the splash, she unsnapped her seat belt and hit redial on her phone, then screamed to her confused fiancé, “I’m in a lake!” Within seconds, the call dropped. She and her unborn baby were all alone in a car that was listing, front driver’s side first, into a body of water.
Around this time, 29-year-old sport fisherman Logan Hayes of Sebastian, Florida, was driving down the same stretch of I-95 in his pickup, remarking to his friend and boss in the passenger seat, Chase Cornell, about how unusual it was that traffic was light and that they were running 20 minutes ahead of schedule on their work errand. “Something’s gonna happen,” Hayes joked.
Sure enough, Hayes soon saw brake lights ahead of him. And then the reason for the sudden slowdown: the Elantra, barely floating in the water.
Other cars had pulled over, but so far nobody had gotten out to help. So Hayes, also a professional surfer and confident swimmer, crossed from the far left lane across two other lanes, cutting off every car in his way, then pulled onto the shoulder and leaped out of the truck.
“Hey, is someone in that car?” he asked a bystander.
“Yeah, the lady’s still in there.”
Hayes ran 50 yards down the highway, then a few more feet to the water’s edge, his eyes fixed on the Elantra. He was shedding clothing every step of the way. Off came his hat, his sunglasses, his shirt, his fishing boots, his sweatpants, his socks … until all he had on were his board shorts.
The outdoor temperature was in the mid-40s when Hayes hit the water around 8 a.m., and the pond was colder than that. But Hayes was surging with adrenaline and didn’t feel the chill as he dove in, trying to cover the distance as quickly as he could. He was underwater for a couple of seconds, then came up and took a few more strokes, and he was at the car.
With the vehicle tipping forward and to the left, the rear passenger door was the only one not submerged. Treading water, he pulled on the door handle, and it flew open. Scared and still struggling to get her bearings, Apollon was jolted by the sight of Hayes floating just outside her suddenly wide-open back door. “You have to get out of the car right now!” he yelled to her.
“How?” she responded.
“You need to!” he urged. “You need to get to me.”
Apollon saw she’d have to crawl over the console between the seats—not easy to do in a car listing in the opposite direction, especially as her instinct was to move delicately and protect her belly. She swung her legs around so her feet were pointing toward Hayes. Now lying on her side, she pushed with her arms and slid up the console, inching toward the back seat, gravity working against her at every turn.
Once her belly cleared the console, she rolled another quarter-turn to her knees, with her stomach toward the floor, and now Hayes could reach her. He pulled her toward him, her back against his chest in the open door of the car. And when he wrapped his arms around her waist, that’s when he realized. Oh, boy. She’s pregnant.
Hayes pulled her most of the way out of the vehicle, but then Apollon’s ankle got caught in the door. “I could feel both of us starting to go down with the car,” he recalls. There wasn’t time to assess exactly how she was stuck or to delicately maneuver her free. He pressed both his feet against the car for leverage, held Apollon tight and pulled steadily until her ankle came free. Then he kicked off against the car as forcefully as he could, his arms wrapped around her. Within 30 seconds, the car was underwater.
Apollon describes herself as a “survival floater”—in other words, not a strong swimmer. And being pregnant didn’t help. Thankfully, as a surfer, Hayes had experience pulling people back to shore. He frog-kicked them both to the edge of the pond, where bystanders helped Apollon out and wrapped her in warm blankets.
But the shock and time spent in the frigid water took its toll. Apollon was seizing convulsively and struggling to maintain consciousness.When local fire and rescue units arrived minutes later, they whisked her off to a nearby hospital, where she endured an emergency cesarean section.
Hayes found out later that day, via text, that Ivory Atara Sully had been born at just 3 pounds, 14 ounces, premature but healthy, and forever sharing a birthday with her mom, who, by then, had recovered.
Hayes and the family have stayed in touch ever since, though he had to wait to meet Ivory in person. She had to spend the first 38 days of her life in the NICU before being introduced to the man who had pulled her and her mom from that sinking car.
Speaking of which, how did Hayes unwind after the ordeal? “I had an incredible surf session,” he says. As for Apollon, she’s already thinking ahead to when Ivory gets a sibling someday. “I just can’t imagine what a normal pregnancy would look like,” she says with a laugh. “I feel like this was such a dramatic entrance, the next one has to top it.”

articles.title: Here’s Why We All Revert to Our Middle School Selves at a Family Holiday Dinner—And How to Cut It Out
articles.content:
The turkey hasn’t even been carved yet and your mom is already complaining that your father “breathes too loud,” your father is giving a dissertation on why you should have bought your car instead of leasing it, and your brother is piling his plate so high with the mashed potatoes that you know there will be none left by the time the bowl makes it to your side of the table. And before you know it, you’re rolling your eyes so hard you can practically see your frontal lobe, you’ve hurled your napkin at your brother, and “Oh! My! God!” has come flying out of your mouth as you resist the urge to stomp away from the table.
You’re an adult. You run meetings, pay bills, have kids of your own. So how did you end up 12 again in less than 30 seconds?
If it makes you feel any better, you’re in good company … and there’s plenty you can do about it. To find out what, exactly, we talked to Tasha Seiter, PhD, a licensed marriage and family therapist and the founder of Heart of the Matter Therapy in Fort Collins, Colorado, and John Mayer, PhD, a clinical psychologist and the author of Family Fit.
Read on to find out why your family can still push your buttons like no one else, what this emotional regression is all about and how to stay the grown-up at the table this year.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, family, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Short answer: You’re back with the people who knew you at 12, and part of you is still stuck in that phase. Yes, even all these years later. “The holidays evoke such strong, visceral regressive emotions in all of us,” Mayer says. “These intense emotions have been imprinted inside us since we were toddlers, so we can’t help but re-experience them throughout our lives.” His name for it? Imprinted regression.
Seiter calls it role regression. “It is also a subtle form of a trauma response—whether it’s big T or little t trauma—where our bodies remember the old roles and scripts we played in our families,” she says. “For example, you might become the responsible one again as you do all of the chores, or the baby, who finds themselves asking for help that they don’t need, or the rebel, breaking the hidden family rules.”
But why do we slip into those parts, even when we know better? “We learned when we were young how to protect ourselves from harm, and our body still has the feeling that we need to play out our adaptations, even when we are adults and no longer need to,” Seiter says.
And no amount of personal growth makes you immune. As Seiter points out, the spiritual teacher Ram Dass famously said, “If you think you’re so enlightened, go spend a week with your family.”
“Let” is doing a lot of heavy lifting there. There’s a confluence of things happening that contribute to this perfect storm of family drama.
Your family pulls you back into these roles. “It is important to understand the power of families,” Mayer says. “As a coping mechanism, families place members in such categories, and often they are immovable.” No matter what you’ve accomplished since you moved out, he explains, “the power of the family forces you in that role.” In fact, if you’ve become more educated, accomplished or social than the rest of your family, keeping you in your childhood role may be how they cope with the difference.
Big events exacerbate issues. It’s not just holidays. Weddings and other family gatherings can trigger this regression too. “It is just that the holidays come around predictably and regularly,” Mayer says, “and these other events don’t.”
Family pecking order can influence how this all plays out. Mayer notes that research hasn’t backed up the famous birth-order personality types. But some families do develop their own patterns around who’s oldest or youngest, and those patterns are “idiosyncratic to families, not any biological imperative,” he says.
Slights sting more when they come from family. “Our relationships with our parents and siblings are our first attachment relationships,” Seiter explains. “When we were young, our very survival depended on these people. If we were not approved of, our brain registered this as a threat to our survival. We still feel these raw spots as adults.”
No wonder the holidays put so many of us on edge. In a November 2025 American Psychiatric Association Healthy Minds Poll, nearly 1 in 3 adults (32%) said they were worried about dealing with challenging family dynamics over the holidays.
Your brain’s alarm system takes over, and the part of your brain that helps you think before you speak goes offline. Yes, a whole lot of science goes into that huff, puff and eye roll. According to Mayer, here’s roughly how it plays out.
Your body gets in on it too. The emotional reaction comes first, Mayer explains, and then the body follows: Blood is diverted away from the digestive tract, your heart rate quickens, your muscles tighten, you might shake, and your blood pressure rises. “This is not a good state of affairs to be in,” he says.
You can’t stop it entirely, but a little prep goes a long way, and so does remembering that the role you’ve slipped into isn’t the real you. These are “temporary feelings and roles and do not define who you are in the rest of your life,” Mayer says.
“First, before the gathering, identify the triggers that usually end up getting to you,” Seiter says. Maybe it’s the way your sister boasts about her kids’ accomplishments. Or the way your grandma eyes you when you reach for that second piece of pie. “Knowing your triggers can help you separate when they actually happen and take a step back,” she says.
Mayer recommends this visualization technique: Picture the event ahead of time, and rehearse exactly how it will go. This will help you walk in prepared instead of ambushed.
Decide in advance how long you’ll stay, and stick to it. Also, set boundaries, and don’t accept, enable or indulge negativity directed at you. And if you’re traveling, think twice before bunking in your childhood bedroom. “People, please, don’t set yourself up for failure,” Mayer says. His most common advice: “Stay in a hotel rather than in a relative’s house.”
When the comment you’ve been dreading lands, a breezy, prepared response keeps you from taking the bait. Seiter suggests:
Seiter suggests practicing what she calls healthy dissociation. “Try to picture yourself as somebody watching a funny—and sometimes scary—movie,” she says. “Enjoy the show without getting swept up in the plot or the plights of the main character. The ridiculousness of it all can sometimes help.” When you feel yourself sliding into eye-rolling mode, she adds, “notice how a younger part of you is being activated to try to protect yourself, and reassure it that you don’t need to get sucked into it.”
The biggest ones tend to reopen old wounds or put you back in a role you’ve outgrown. Every family is different, but Mayer says these are the triggers he hears about most.
Call a grown-up time-out. At 12, you got sent to your room. Now you get to step away on your own terms, without slamming a single door. Here are some helpful tips.
If you catch it early, you may not need to go anywhere. “Everyone has a personal tell that they are flooded,” Seiter says. “It may be a faster heart rate, heat in the body or a feeling of irritability.” When you notice yours, she suggests, “bring your attention back to your breath, and make your exhales longer than your inhales. Notice your feet on the floor, and name three things in the room that are your favorite color.”
“The initial surge can last just 90 seconds,” Seiter says. “But if we end up getting flooded, it takes the body a full 20 minutes to calm down and return to baseline. This is research from John Gottman based on heart-rate monitors.” Use that time to move. “The best way to let off steam is to go for a walk or otherwise move your body,” she says. Talking to someone you trust or journaling can help too, as long as it’s not just endlessly venting.
“No fanfare—just fade back into the event,” Mayer says. He suggests staying on the sidelines for a while until things settle.
Once your prefrontal cortex (and your adult self) is back online, own what happened. “Before you explain yourself, acknowledge where you went wrong, and name what you will do to make it right,” Seiter says. For example: “I really overreacted there, and I know it. I don’t want to be that person, and I’m sorry. I’m going to work on my reactivity.”
The key is skipping the defensiveness. Getting defensive, she says, “only creates a pattern where the other person tries harder—and gets louder—to feel heard.”
You don’t have to fix your whole family before dessert. “Members of your family will likely always have limitations,” Seiter explains. “You don’t have to love every part of them.” That said, changing how you respond can make a difference. “If one person in the family learns to respond differently, it does have a ripple effect on the entire system,” she says, though she warns that families tend to resist change at first, so expect some pushback.
And if a relative is truly hurtful, you don’t owe them a seat next to you just because it’s a holiday. “If Uncle Charlie is a negative, abusive, hurtful relative, don’t force yourself to deal with him just because of the holidays,” Mayer says. Showing up for that treatment doesn’t help them either. “You want them to change?” he posits. “Don’t reinforce their behavior.”
Seiter agrees that in cases of abuse, going no contact may be the healthiest option, and a therapist can help you figure out what’s right for you. For everyone else, there’s always the gravy pass.

Watch it like a movie

Seiter suggests practicing what she calls healthy dissociation. “Try to picture yourself as somebody watching a funny—and sometimes scary—movie,” she says. “Enjoy the show without getting swept up in the plot or the plights of the main character. The ridiculousness of it all can sometimes help.” When you feel yourself sliding into eye-rolling mode, she adds, “notice how a younger part of you is being activated to try to protect yourself, and reassure it that you don’t need to get sucked into it.”

What triggers should you watch out for?

The biggest ones tend to reopen old wounds or put you back in a role you’ve outgrown. Every family is different, but Mayer says these are the triggers he hears about most.

  • Old fights, reheated. The argument that never really ended gets picked right back up between the turkey and the pie.
  • Negative or hurtful relatives. The critical aunt or the uncle who always goes too far can make you feel small all over again.
  • Being shoved back into a role that hurts. Maybe you were the screwup, the invisible one or the one who had to keep everyone happy, and you’re expected to play that part again.
  • Your kids watching you get disrespected. It’s one thing to get talked down to. It’s another when your children see it.
  • Your kids being treated as less than the other grandkids. Favoritism toward the cousins can bring out your fiercest middle schooler.

OK, so you took the bait. Now what?

Call a grown-up time-out. At 12, you got sent to your room. Now you get to step away on your own terms, without slamming a single door. Here are some helpful tips.

Calm down without leaving the table

If you catch it early, you may not need to go anywhere. “Everyone has a personal tell that they are flooded,” Seiter says. “It may be a faster heart rate, heat in the body or a feeling of irritability.” When you notice yours, she suggests, “bring your attention back to your breath, and make your exhales longer than your inhales. Notice your feet on the floor, and name three things in the room that are your favorite color.”

Give it 20 minutes

“The initial surge can last just 90 seconds,” Seiter says. “But if we end up getting flooded, it takes the body a full 20 minutes to calm down and return to baseline. This is research from John Gottman based on heart-rate monitors.” Use that time to move. “The best way to let off steam is to go for a walk or otherwise move your body,” she says. Talking to someone you trust or journaling can help too, as long as it’s not just endlessly venting.

Slip back in quietly

“No fanfare—just fade back into the event,” Mayer says. He suggests staying on the sidelines for a while until things settle.

Repair it

Once your prefrontal cortex (and your adult self) is back online, own what happened. “Before you explain yourself, acknowledge where you went wrong, and name what you will do to make it right,” Seiter says. For example: “I really overreacted there, and I know it. I don’t want to be that person, and I’m sorry. I’m going to work on my reactivity.”

The key is skipping the defensiveness. Getting defensive, she says, “only creates a pattern where the other person tries harder—and gets louder—to feel heard.”

The bottom line

You don’t have to fix your whole family before dessert. “Members of your family will likely always have limitations,” Seiter explains. “You don’t have to love every part of them.” That said, changing how you respond can make a difference. “If one person in the family learns to respond differently, it does have a ripple effect on the entire system,” she says, though she warns that families tend to resist change at first, so expect some pushback.

And if a relative is truly hurtful, you don’t owe them a seat next to you just because it’s a holiday. “If Uncle Charlie is a negative, abusive, hurtful relative, don’t force yourself to deal with him just because of the holidays,” Mayer says. Showing up for that treatment doesn’t help them either. “You want them to change?” he posits. “Don’t reinforce their behavior.”

Seiter agrees that in cases of abuse, going no contact may be the healthiest option, and a therapist can help you figure out what’s right for you. For everyone else, there’s always the gravy pass.

  • Tasha Seiter, PhD, LMFT, is a licensed marriage and family therapist and the founder of Heart of the Matter Therapy in Fort Collins, Colorado. She also conducts research at Colorado State University and writes for Psychology Today.
  • John Mayer, PhD, is a clinical psychologist and professor. He is the author of Family Fit: Find Your Balance.

articles.title: Hating How Early It Gets Dark? Try Cozymaxxing, the Feel-Good Trend That’ll Make You Look Forward to Nighttime
articles.content:
I hadn’t meal-prepped in months. There was a Netflix show I’d been meaning to watch, chores were piling up, and my partner and I hadn’t had much time for a quiet night together. Between work and everything else on my schedule, I was struggling to find time for much of anything.
The change in seasons wasn’t helping. By the time I finished work, it was already dark outside, and whatever motivation I had left seemed to disappear with the daylight. I was tired, had plenty to catch up on and somehow felt guilty about wanting to spend what little free time I had relaxing.
So when I came across cozymaxxing, a social media trend that encourages people to make their time at home as comfortable and enjoyable as possible, the timing couldn’t have been better. And when I learned that some of the ideas behind it overlap with an established treatment for seasonal depression, I wondered if there might be more to it than an excuse to stay home.
To find out, I spoke with a psychologist who’s spent decades researching winter depression, then gave cozymaxxing a try for three evenings. Read on to find out how my cozy little experiment went—and why you’re going to want to hop right on this cozy train.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more trends, psychology, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Cozymaxxing means deliberately making your surroundings and activities as comfortable and relaxing as possible. Think: candles, blankets, warm drinks and spending an evening doing whatever sounds good to you.
The trend gained attention in 2025 through videos of cozy living-room setups, cooking, reading and movie nights. As of November 2026, more than 500 Instagram posts feature the #cozymaxxing hashtag, with some videos racking up as many as 3.4 million views.
Dictionary.com named maxxing its 2026 Word of the Year, recognizing the growing number of trends dedicated to optimizing everything from appearance (looksmaxxing) to sleep (sleepmaxxing). Cozymaxxing is a funny addition to the bunch, considering how little effort it asks of you.
Cozymaxxing may help improve your mood by giving you something to look forward to during a season that can leave you feeling tired and unmotivated.
Kelly Rohan, PhD, a psychology professor at the University of Vermont who studies seasonal depression, says it’s common to notice changes in your mood and energy as the days get shorter. Some people barely feel the difference, while others develop seasonal affective disorder (SAD), a form of clinical depression that typically occurs during the fall and winter. Many of us fall somewhere in between, feeling more tired, sleeping longer or noticing changes in our appetite.
Shorter days appear to be a major reason why. According to the National Institute of Mental Health, people with SAD may experience changes in serotonin and melatonin, chemicals involved in regulating mood and sleep. These changes can also throw off the body’s internal clock, although researchers are still figuring out exactly how it all works.
Rohan has spent 25 years studying cognitive behavioral therapy for winter depression. One technique she uses is called behavioral activation, which encourages people to get out and do something they normally like, even when they aren’t feeling up to it. “Anything that one can do to approach and embrace the winter season and find some joy in it is probably going to be helpful for well-being and mental health,” she says.
She’s even encouraged patients to try things that sound a lot like cozymaxxing, including taking warm baths surrounded by candles. Rohan says it can help to find things you genuinely like about winter, similar to how you might look forward to gardening, swimming or spending time outdoors in the summer. She also points to Scandinavian traditions like hygge, which encourage people to embrace the colder months by making their homes warm and inviting.
Of course, cozymaxxing hasn’t been studied as a treatment for depression. But Rohan’s research offers a good reason to make some plans for those dark winter evenings—even if your plans don’t involve leaving the house.
There are plenty of ways to cozymaxx, and you probably already have everything you need at home. Here are a few ideas to get started.
You can combine a few of these throughout the evening or stick with one. Whatever you choose, there’s no need to recreate the elaborate setups you might see on Instagram.
I started by catching up on a few things I’d been meaning to do, including binge-watching The Body on Netflix (10/10 recommend). I also started putting together a bedtime routine for the winter, making myself a cup of tea, slipping on an eye mask and listening to an audiobook before bed. I’d wanted to get into the habit of winding down earlier, but I hadn’t made much of an effort to actually do it.
I carved out time for chores, because being responsible can be cozy too, especially if you’re wearing slippers. For the first time in months, I meal-prepped, making a big pot of hearty vegetarian chili and some cornbread muffins (courtesy of Dolly Parton’s store-bought mix, the only one I’d trust over a homemade recipe). I love cooking, but it’s usually one of the first things to fall off my to-do list when life gets hectic. This time, I could take my time in the kitchen, and I had dinner taken care of for the rest of the week.
I made room for some actual rest too. I lit candles, put on quiet music and took a long bath. I used a hair oil ritual set and then a heated massage gadget on my shoulders. I’d been so caught up in everything else that I hadn’t been paying much attention to the toll stress was taking on my body, and it felt heavenly to give myself a little extra care.
My partner and I spent another evening playing video games, watching Survivor and working on a painting kit side by side. We’d both needed some quality time together, but we weren’t up to planning an elaborate date night. We could stay in, paint and watch people argue on a deserted island. (We’re Team Sharonda in this house.)
After three nights of cozymaxxing, I felt a lot less guilty about taking time for myself. I had been so busy lately that my evenings had started to feel like an extension of my workday, with one thing to finish after another. It was nice to spend a few nights doing whatever I felt like doing for a change.
What surprised me, though, was how much easier it was to relax once I’d made plans to do exactly that. Normally, even when I’m exhausted, I find myself thinking about what else I could squeeze into the evening. But this time, I wasn’t running through my to-do list while I watched TV or wondering whether I should be doing something more useful. I’d already decided how I wanted to spend those hours.
I’m hoping to set aside one evening a week for cozymaxxing this winter, even if all I do is make dinner, put on my pajamas and watch TV with my partner. I know how quickly those hours can fill up when I’m busy, and I’d rather make plans to enjoy them now than wait until I’m completely exhausted to give myself another night off.
Absolutely. You can work little bits of cozymaxxing into your regular day, even when you don’t have a whole evening free.
Try setting aside 15 minutes to read, having your morning coffee somewhere comfortable or listening to a podcast while making dinner. A few small changes to your surroundings, like softer lighting or a warm blanket while you work, can also make your usual routines feel a little cozier. My editor, who works from home, has started lighting a candle and donning big, fluffy socks while doing her normal tasks; she says it’s made a huge difference to her mood and productivity, giving her that extra boost when it feels like midnight at 5 p.m.
If you’re having trouble making time for yourself, take a page from Rohan’s approach to scheduling activities. Pick something you’d like to do and decide when you’re going to do it, rather than hoping you’ll somehow find the time later.
Yes, especially if staying home starts replacing social contact or becomes a way to withdraw from activities you usually enjoy. Rohan cautions that for someone experiencing depression, spending long periods on the couch without anything to occupy their attention can lead to rumination or getting caught in repetitive negative thoughts.
She also emphasizes the importance of maintaining relationships. “Social activities can be particularly mood enhancing,” she says. Having a friend over for dinner or planning a movie night with your partner can be a good way to spend time with other people without giving up the comforts of home.
Cozymaxxing also isn’t a treatment for SAD. If low mood persists or interferes with your daily life, Rohan recommends speaking with a health-care professional. Effective treatments include light therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy and medication.
For me, the earlier sunsets are still taking some getting used to. But I’ve spent enough evenings feeling like the day was over as soon as I closed my laptop. I’m looking forward to making better use of those hours this winter, even if some nights that means doing very little at all.

articles.title: Fresh vs. Frozen vs. Canned Vegetables: Which Is Better? (Hint: It May Not Be the One You Think!)
articles.content:
We were always taught—or maybe we just assumed?—that fresh produce was always the best choice. That it’s the healthiest, the best-tasting, the whole nine yards. But remember this summer, when fresh produce was trying to kill us? And what about all the soups and casseroles and holiday dishes we’re making right now that call for frozen or canned veggies? Why are we so obsessed with fresh?
Samantha Peterson, a functional medicine dietitian and personal trainer, has a theory. “Fresh feels closest to nature. We see crisp lettuce and bright peppers in the produce section and immediately read them as healthy, while anything in a bag or a can feels ‘processed,’” she says. “That word has been used so broadly that it now scares people away.”
Should it? Or should we stop being so snobby about our veggies and start feeling good about them in whatever form they come in? Of course, it’s complicated … but we’re here to make it easy for you. Read on as we settle the fresh vs. frozen vs. canned debate once and for all.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food, holidays, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
As noted above, most people believe fresh equals healthy. But the word fresh just describes how a vegetable looks, not how long ago it was picked, which is the real marker of how many nutrients it contains when it reaches your plate, Peterson says. Veggies develop nutrients while they’re ripening, she explains, so those that are picked too early are starting at a deficit. But once they’re picked, the clock starts.
“Vegetables keep ‘breathing’ after they’re picked, and delicate nutrients like vitamin C and folate start to break down with time, heat and light. Leafy greens like spinach are especially sensitive,” Peterson says. “So how far a vegetable traveled, and how long it sat in a warehouse, a store and your fridge, matters as much as how it was grown.” Put another way, a fresh veggie that has been off the plant for more than a week is going to contain fewer nutrients than one that was frozen the same day it was picked.
Of course, there are other factors besides nutrient content that determine whether you want a fresh, frozen or canned vegetable. Things like taste, cost, seasonality, waste and more all play a role too, as you’ll see below.
OK, it’s the moment of truth. Here’s what you need to know before your next trip to the grocery store.
Pros: If you can get your hands on in-season, just-picked fresh veggies, you can’t beat them for nutrient content, flavor and texture. “Fresh is the only option that gives you real crunch, which makes it ideal for salads, slaws, crudités and snacking,” Peterson says. Many vitamins and minerals, such as vitamin C, are sensitive to heat, so eating fresh veggies ensures that you are getting the full possible amount of those vitamins from the food.”
You also have full control over how the veggies are prepared. “There’s no added salt, sauce or seasoning unless you add it,” Peterson notes.
Cons: The biggest downside to fresh produce is its short shelf life. “Most of us have opened the crisper drawer to find a bag of wilted spinach we had big plans for,” says Peterson. “Fresh produce goes bad quickly, and tossing it wastes both food and money.”
Speaking of cost, both the price and quality of fresh veggies are going to vary widely depending on the time of year. “A winter tomato is often pale, mealy and more expensive than a summer one,” Peterson says.
And since fresh veggies are (usually) whole and raw, they take more time to prepare than their frozen and canned counterparts.
Pros: Frozen vegetables are loaded with nutrients. “They’re typically picked at peak ripeness and frozen within hours, which locks in their nutrition at its high point,” Peterson explains. “Research comparing the two has found frozen vegetables are often nutritionally similar to fresh, and sometimes higher than fresh produce that’s been stored in the fridge for several days.”
They also last much, much longer than fresh veggies, which is more cost-effective and limits waste. “They’re already washed and chopped, prices stay fairly steady year-round, and you can get summer vegetables in January,” Peterson says. “They work beautifully in stir-fries, soups, sheet-pan dinners and grain bowls. “
Cons: Just as texture is one of the biggest perks of a fresh veggie, it’s the primary downside to a frozen one. “Ice crystals soften the vegetable’s cell walls, so frozen vegetables won’t give you the crunch you want in a salad,” Peterson explains. “They can turn mushy if boiled, which is why I recommend roasting or sautéing them straight from frozen instead.”
Plus, some frozen products may have a picture of plain veggies on the front, only to contain sauce, seasoning, butter or cheese that adds sodium, saturated fat or something else you don’t want mixed up with your veggies.
Finally, freezer space is tight for most people, and keeping a variety of frozen veggies on hand will take up a lot of it.
Pros: Of the three varieties of veggies, canned are the most budget-friendly, the most shelf-stable and the easiest to store. “They’re already cooked, so they’re ready in minutes, and they make a great pantry backup for weeks when fresh food runs low or time is limited,” says Peterson. “For many families, canned vegetables are the most affordable and accessible way to get vegetables on the table, and that matters.”
While some vitamins break down with the addition of heat, certain antioxidants in vegetables actually become easier for your body to absorb after they are exposed to the heat of canning, Peterson explains. “Lycopene in tomatoes and beta-carotene in carrots and pumpkin are good examples,” she says. “Fiber and minerals hold up well during canning too.”
Cons: Sodium content is the most prominent one. “Regular canned vegetables often contain added salt, which adds up quickly if you’re eating them often,” says Peterson, adding that those heat-sensitive vitamins like C and B do tend to be lower in canned veggies.
“Texture and flavor may also be impacted,” she adds. “Canned vegetables are softer, the colors are more muted, and some people notice a slightly metallic taste.”
Finally, canned vegetables tend to offer a more limited variety than fresh or frozen, and there have been some concerns about BPA in the lining of cans. “Many brands have moved away from it, so if that’s a priority for you, look for cans labeled BPA-free,” Peterson suggests.
If it seems to you like there isn’t a clear winner in this debate, you’d be correct. “But if I had to pick the option that checks the most boxes for nutrition, cost, convenience and waste, frozen comes out on top,” Peterson says. The only thing frozen veggies can’t do is be served raw and crunchy in a salad or on a snack spread.
That’s why it’s worth keeping all three in your rotation, Peterson says. Here’s what that can look like on a daily and seasonal basis: “In the summer, buy fresh tomatoes, cucumbers and corn at their peak, and enjoy them raw or lightly cooked. On a busy weeknight, grab a bag of frozen stir-fry vegetables and have dinner ready in 15 minutes. For chili, soups and pasta sauce, canned tomatoes are hard to beat. If you live alone or cook for one, frozen vegetables let you use a handful at a time without watching the rest go bad. And for salads or snacking, stick with fresh for that satisfying crunch.”
But the real winner is the one you and your family are going to eat. “Only about 1 in 10 adults in the U.S. eats enough vegetables, so the bigger win is getting more of them on your plate, in any form,” Peterson says.
Yes, this Thanksgiving classic typically relies on canned green beans. Which as you may have guessed by now, is A-OK, as long as you’re being discerning about the cans you choose.
First, Peterson suggests looking for a can that says “no salt added” or “low sodium” on the front, which guarantees fewer than 140 milligrams of sodium per serving, and avoiding ones that say “reduced sodium,” which will still be pretty high. “Then flip to the nutrition facts label,” she says. “A daily value of 5% or less for sodium is considered low, and 20% or more is high.”
Finally, take a look at the ingredients list. For green beans, or any veggies for that matter, you’ll want to choose a can that contains only the vegetable, water and maybe salt—nothing else. “And whatever you buy, drain and rinse the beans before using them; it’s a simple step that washes away some of the sodium,” Peterson adds.
If you’re having trouble finding low-sodium green beans, especially for green bean casserole that contains other high-sodium ingredients like cream of mushroom soup, Peterson suggests using frozen instead. “They’re a great swap, and they hold up beautifully in the oven,” she promises. We were always taught—or maybe we just assumed?—that fresh produce was always the best choice. That it’s the healthiest, the best-tasting, the whole nine yards. But remember this summer, when fresh produce was trying to kill us? And what about all the soups and casseroles and holiday dishes we’re making right now that call for frozen or canned veggies? Why are we so obsessed with fresh?

Samantha Peterson, a functional medicine dietitian and personal trainer, has a theory. “Fresh feels closest to nature. We see crisp lettuce and bright peppers in the produce section and immediately read them as healthy, while anything in a bag or a can feels ‘processed,’” she says. “That word has been used so broadly that it now scares people away.”

Should it? Or should we stop being so snobby about our veggies and start feeling good about them in whatever form they come in? Of course, it’s complicated … but we’re here to make it easy for you. Read on as we settle the fresh vs. frozen vs. canned debate once and for all.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food, holidays, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

What’s at the root of the fresh vs. frozen vs. canned veggie debate?

As noted above, most people believe fresh equals healthy. But the word fresh just describes how a vegetable looks, not how long ago it was picked, which is the real marker of how many nutrients it contains when it reaches your plate, Peterson says. Veggies develop nutrients while they’re ripening, she explains, so those that are picked too early are starting at a deficit. But once they’re picked, the clock starts.

“Vegetables keep ‘breathing’ after they’re picked, and delicate nutrients like vitamin C and folate start to break down with time, heat and light. Leafy greens like spinach are especially sensitive,” Peterson says. “So how far a vegetable traveled, and how long it sat in a warehouse, a store and your fridge, matters as much as how it was grown.” Put another way, a fresh veggie that has been off the plant for more than a week is going to contain fewer nutrients than one that was frozen the same day it was picked.

Of course, there are other factors besides nutrient content that determine whether you want a fresh, frozen or canned vegetable. Things like taste, cost, seasonality, waste and more all play a role too, as you’ll see below.

What are the pros and cons of each type of vegetable choice?

OK, it’s the moment of truth. Here’s what you need to know before your next trip to the grocery store.

Fresh vegetables

Pros: If you can get your hands on in-season, just-picked fresh veggies, you can’t beat them for nutrient content, flavor and texture. “Fresh is the only option that gives you real crunch, which makes it ideal for salads, slaws, crudités and snacking,” Peterson says. Many vitamins and minerals, such as vitamin C, are sensitive to heat, so eating fresh veggies ensures that you are getting the full possible amount of those vitamins from the food.”

You also have full control over how the veggies are prepared. “There’s no added salt, sauce or seasoning unless you add it,” Peterson notes.

Cons: The biggest downside to fresh produce is its short shelf life. “Most of us have opened the crisper drawer to find a bag of wilted spinach we had big plans for,” says Peterson. “Fresh produce goes bad quickly, and tossing it wastes both food and money.”

Speaking of cost, both the price and quality of fresh veggies are going to vary widely depending on the time of year. “A winter tomato is often pale, mealy and more expensive than a summer one,” Peterson says.

And since fresh veggies are (usually) whole and raw, they take more time to prepare than their frozen and canned counterparts.

Frozen vegetables

Pros: Frozen vegetables are loaded with nutrients. “They’re typically picked at peak ripeness and frozen within hours, which locks in their nutrition at its high point,” Peterson explains. “Research comparing the two has found frozen vegetables are often nutritionally similar to fresh, and sometimes higher than fresh produce that’s been stored in the fridge for several days.”

They also last much, much longer than fresh veggies, which is more cost-effective and limits waste. “They’re already washed and chopped, prices stay fairly steady year-round, and you can get summer vegetables in January,” Peterson says. “They work beautifully in stir-fries, soups, sheet-pan dinners and grain bowls. “

Cons: Just as texture is one of the biggest perks of a fresh veggie, it’s the primary downside to a frozen one. “Ice crystals soften the vegetable’s cell walls, so frozen vegetables won’t give you the crunch you want in a salad,” Peterson explains. “They can turn mushy if boiled, which is why I recommend roasting or sautéing them straight from frozen instead.”

Plus, some frozen products may have a picture of plain veggies on the front, only to contain sauce, seasoning, butter or cheese that adds sodium, saturated fat or something else you don’t want mixed up with your veggies.

Finally, freezer space is tight for most people, and keeping a variety of frozen veggies on hand will take up a lot of it.

Canned vegetables

Pros: Of the three varieties of veggies, canned are the most budget-friendly, the most shelf-stable and the easiest to store. “They’re already cooked, so they’re ready in minutes, and they make a great pantry backup for weeks when fresh food runs low or time is limited,” says Peterson. “For many families, canned vegetables are the most affordable and accessible way to get vegetables on the table, and that matters.”

While some vitamins break down with the addition of heat, certain antioxidants in vegetables actually become easier for your body to absorb after they are exposed to the heat of canning, Peterson explains. “Lycopene in tomatoes and beta-carotene in carrots and pumpkin are good examples,” she says. “Fiber and minerals hold up well during canning too.”

Cons: Sodium content is the most prominent one. “Regular canned vegetables often contain added salt, which adds up quickly if you’re eating them often,” says Peterson, adding that those heat-sensitive vitamins like C and B do tend to be lower in canned veggies.

“Texture and flavor may also be impacted,” she adds. “Canned vegetables are softer, the colors are more muted, and some people notice a slightly metallic taste.”

Finally, canned vegetables tend to offer a more limited variety than fresh or frozen, and there have been some concerns about BPA in the lining of cans. “Many brands have moved away from it, so if that’s a priority for you, look for cans labeled BPA-free,” Peterson suggests.

So which is the winner?

If it seems to you like there isn’t a clear winner in this debate, you’d be correct. “But if I had to pick the option that checks the most boxes for nutrition, cost, convenience and waste, frozen comes out on top,” Peterson says. The only thing frozen veggies can’t do is be served raw and crunchy in a salad or on a snack spread.

That’s why it’s worth keeping all three in your rotation, Peterson says. Here’s what that can look like on a daily and seasonal basis: “In the summer, buy fresh tomatoes, cucumbers and corn at their peak, and enjoy them raw or lightly cooked. On a busy weeknight, grab a bag of frozen stir-fry vegetables and have dinner ready in 15 minutes. For chili, soups and pasta sauce, canned tomatoes are hard to beat. If you live alone or cook for one, frozen vegetables let you use a handful at a time without watching the rest go bad. And for salads or snacking, stick with fresh for that satisfying crunch.”

But the real winner is the one you and your family are going to eat. “Only about 1 in 10 adults in the U.S. eats enough vegetables, so the bigger win is getting more of them on your plate, in any form,” Peterson says.

What does this mean for your famous green bean casserole?

Yes, this Thanksgiving classic typically relies on canned green beans. Which as you may have guessed by now, is A-OK, as long as you’re being discerning about the cans you choose.

First, Peterson suggests looking for a can that says “no salt added” or “low sodium” on the front, which guarantees fewer than 140 milligrams of sodium per serving, and avoiding ones that say “reduced sodium,” which will still be pretty high. “Then flip to the nutrition facts label,” she says. “A daily value of 5% or less for sodium is considered low, and 20% or more is high.”

Finally, take a look at the ingredients list. For green beans, or any veggies for that matter, you’ll want to choose a can that contains only the vegetable, water and maybe salt—nothing else. “And whatever you buy, drain and rinse the beans before using them; it’s a simple step that washes away some of the sodium,” Peterson adds.

If you’re having trouble finding low-sodium green beans, especially for green bean casserole that contains other high-sodium ingredients like cream of mushroom soup, Peterson suggests using frozen instead. “They’re a great swap, and they hold up beautifully in the oven,” she promises. Your guests will be none the wiser.

articles.title: Thousands of Units of Toothpaste and Mouthwash Are Being Recalled Due to Unwanted Hormones Found in Product Samples—Here’s the Full List
articles.content:
When you think about product recalls, toothpaste and mouthwash probably aren’t the first things that come to mind. We’re used to hearing about recalls involving food, cars and household products, but everyday oral care items can make the list, too. This latest recall is a reminder that even products families use as part of their daily routines aren’t automatically free from safety concerns.
Thousands of toothpaste and mouthwash products made for children and adults are being recalled after testing uncovered hormone contamination, according to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
The voluntary recall involves 51,762 units of six ORL Organic Oral Care products distributed nationwide. The FDA notified ORL Labs after testing found hormones in samples of the products, according to its enforcement report.
The recall began Oct. 12 but was classified as a Class II recall earlier this month. That designation means the products may “cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences,” according to the FDA’s recall definitions.
The recall covers the following products. All of the items have expiration dates between September 2026 and August 2028.
Bubblegum Kids natural toothpaste
Cinnamint toothpaste
Fresh Mint natural toothpaste
Bubblegum Kids Mouthwash
Cinnamint Kids Mouthwash
Fresh mint mouthwash
The FDA report says samples contained progesterone, estradiol or dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). It doesn’t identify the amounts found or explain how the cross-contamination happened. It’s the second toothpaste recall as of late, too.
The report also doesn’t specify what consumers should do with products they purchased. Anyone with questions can contact ORL Labs at 844-675-5227 or email orl@orlcares.com.
